language.howToChooseYourGradeIntro: Our curriculum Grades K to 6 corresponds with ages:
language.howToChooseYourGradeContent:
It’s very important children start at the right level, have fun in learning and work at their own pace. Please help the children selecting the level that is not too easy, but also not too difficult for them. There are two ways to do this.

  • You can either check the learning goals yourself to determine the correct level for your child(ren).
  • Or you can let the child take several lessons to determine his or her level. For example, if your child has the age of 6, please let him or her take one lesson in grade K, one lesson in grade 1, and one lesson in grade 2 to determine at which level he or she is.

dialog.text: Hello, I am Tim.
Hi, I’m Sandra. I’m going to run a race. Humans and animals always use their respiratory system to breathe. This is important, because when we breathe in, our lungs collect oxygen from the air.
The oxygen is pumped by our blood through our bodies. When we breathe out, we exhale carbon dioxide, which our body does not need.
When we do physical exercise, like running a race, we have to breathe faster to get more oxygen. This means our respiratory system is working even harder.
Watch Sandra run the race and use her respiratory system to help her breathe harder and faster.
Now, lets learn what parts of our bodies make up our respiratory system, and what they do.

activities.title: Drag the steps into the correct order.
activities.subtitle: Do you know the steps of the respiratory system? (1/2)

answers.text: Air travels down toward the lungs through the trachea.
Inhale and exhale air through your nose and mouth.
Air travels into the Bronchus before it reaches the lungs.

activities.title: Drag the steps into the correct order.
activities.subtitle: Do you know the steps of the respiratory system? (2/2)

answers.text: The Oxygen is exchanged for Carbon Dioxide.
Both lungs collect the inhaled oxygen. Oxygen is transported from lungs to the rest of the body through blood.
Finally, the diaphragm squeezes the lungs up to exhale; the carbon dioxide leaves the body.
